On section 1-persons acting as master and engineer:
Will the minister explain that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The necessity of this Bill arises in consequence of the fact that a great many small boats are now being propelled by combustion engines using gasoline or oil as fuel. When the present Act was passed no such boats.were in use. The Act applies to steamboats, no matter by what means the power is obtained. Under the law at present if any boat carries passengers it must, unless it is not more than five tons in size, have a certificated engineer and a certificated captain. Consequently,

boats that can very well be managed by one man who has the qualifications both of engineer and of master have to employ two men. This has caused a good deal of trouble in different parts of the country, especially in British Columbia. Section 629 of the Act as at present reads:	.
No person shall act in the double capacity of engineer and master on any steamboat, and no person shall, except when the boiler1 is fired from the engine room, act as engineer and fireman on any steamboat having an engine of over seven nominal horse-power and required by law to carry a certificated engineer.
It is proposed to add these words to that section:
Subject to such regulations as may be made by the minister this section shall not apply to any passenger ship not exceeding sixty-five feet registered length propelled by an internal combustion engine, or by a steam engine with a flash boiler, or by electricity.
Under the provisions of this amendment, one man can act as both .master and engineer on board any boat of that description.
What is meant iby the terms "internal combustion engine" and "flash boiler?"

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The internal combustion engines are those in which gasolene or fuel oil is used. They have no boilers, and, of course, do not employ steam. A flash boiler is the special type of boiler used, to produce steam by means of gasolene. The flash of the gasolene heats the boiler and produces the steam.

What are the qualiffications of an engineer on a gasolene boat?
jMr. HAZEN: As the law stands to-day they are exactly the same as those of the engineer of a steamboat. We propose to amend that by the second section of this Bill.

The first section provides that section 629 shall not apply to any passenger ship not exceeding 65 feet registered length, propelled1 by an internal combustion engine, or by an engine with a flash boiler, or by electricity. The second section is limited to internal combustion engines.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The second section does not apply to steam engines with flash boilers.

propelled' by electricity would not be provided fOT.

Among the Thousand Islands there are many small boats not exceeding 65 feet registered length propelled by internal combustion engines or by flash boilers. Those boats carry passengers, but under the regulations, Canadian boats of this type have been forbidden to carry passengers, and the American boat men have had a monopoly of this business. I suppose the same conditions prevail in other international waters.

This is intended to cover everything excepting boats propelled by sails. Will the minister say whether it covers the case of private yachts? In the coastal waters and the inland waters of Canada there are a great many private yachts that carry passengers and go on excursions. Sometimes large numbers are carried on these boats. Is it intended that the Bill should cover such boats as these?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It applies to any vessel that carries passengers which does not exceed 65 feet in length.

It will be readily understood that in. the case of an open boat with a gasolene engine or a flash 'boiler, it is easy for one man to act as -both captain and engineer, and this amendment will permit Canadian owners to carry passengers amon* the Thousand Islands as the Americans do now.

On section 1-number of Quebec pilots:

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This is a very simple
change, though I think a necessary one, in order that fair play may be given to those Who desire to become pilots in the Quebec pilotage district. Before a man can become a licensed pilot, or go up for examination, he has to serve an apprenticeship of seven years, and during that apprenticeship he

has to take several sea voyages to foreign countries. Section 444 of the Act contains a provision that if the apprenticeship of a candidate, for any reason at all, is interrupted for a period of four months, thiat time cannot be made up, and he cannot get his certificate. An apprentice may have served six years, and then, if he is taken ill, or for any unavoidable cause the apprenticeship is interrupted for a period of more than four months, 'he will not be able to. get his certificate, even if: he makes up the time, and even i'f the circumstances which prevented	him	from putting
in the full time have been removed.
The section as it stands at present provides that if the period of apprenticeship of any apprentice becomes interrupted for a longer period than four months, no matter from what cause, it will not be possible for the apprentice to complete his term and obtain his license. By this Bill, apprentices whose period of service may for legitimate reasons be interrupted, will be enabled to make up for such time as has been lost, provided the apprentice is in every other respect found qualified, and has completed the full period of seven years.
This Bill sets no limit to the time an apprentice may be absent?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, but he cannot get his certificate until he has put in the full period of seven years.

This leaves the door
wide open; an apprentice may put in his time to suit himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Oh, no.
Suppose he puts in three years, and then goes to the United States for ten years. This Bill would allow him to put in the other four years at the end of that time, would it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is an age limit for
pilots. I think a man cannot get a pilot's certificate after he is twenty-seven years of age, but I speak subject to correction.
The age limit is the only thing that would prevent him from resuming his apprenticeship in the case I mentioned. Is this Bill intended to apply to some special case that has arisen?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is intended to apply to all cases, hut as a matter of fact a case actually has arisen where a pilot who had served six years faithfu'ly and well met with an accident that interrupted his apprenticeship for a longer period than four months, and consequently, under the law as it now stands, he was unable to continue his apprenticeship. Unless this Bill passes that man could hot get his certificate, even though he went on and put in the whole seven years. That seemed a hardship, and it is for the purpose of meeting such cases that the Bill has been introduced. Cases of this kind rarely happen, however, because when a pilot starts in he generally finishes the course, or abandons it early in his career to pursue some other calling.

As the case
has been explained by my hon. friend, some injustice would apparently be done if this Bill were not passed. I would observe, however, that the Pilot's Corporation has been in existence for forty years, and probably more, and this is the first time that I have heard of any complaint against the existing law. I do not think it at all wise to amend a general law just for the purpose of meeting one particular case. If the Pilots* Corporation has found it to its advantage to have this stern law-and apparently it is a stern law-and has made no complaint, to my certain knowledge, for more than forty years, I do not see any strong reason why the law should be amended to meet just one particular case. Has the Pilots' Corporation been consulted, and does it approve of this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Our attention was called to this matter by the pilots in the Quebec district, who considered it a very grave injustice that this young man, who had put in six years of honest and faithful work, and whose apprenticeship was interrupted through no fault of his own, should not be able to get his certificate. It seems to me that we should not allow such injustice to be done any man.

If the Pilots' Corporation have been consulted, and if this Bill is introduced at their request, I have nothing more to say.
Mr. L'ESPERANCE: It was on the request of the Quebec Pilots' Corporation that I asked the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to introduce this Bill. The particular case which made us think an amendment to the law desirable was that of Camille Couillard, who, after putting in six years of his apprenticeship, met with an accident on one of the voyages abroad which the corporation compels apprentices to take. This young man met with an accident while on

duty in England, as a result of which he was laid up in hospital for nine months, and when he returned to Canada the Quebec Pilots' Corporation could not, under the law as it is at present, allow him to resume his aprenticeship.
If the corporation agrees, I have nothing more to say. I see it says the number of pilots for the district of Quebec shall not exceed 125. Is that the law?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Bill before the House provides that this section 442, dealing with the number of pilots, and sections 443 and 444, shall be repealed. By the provisions of chapter 48 of the Acts of 1914, all the powers with respect to pilots and apprentices, formerly vested in the Quebec Pilots' Corporation, became vested in the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. This was done on the recommendation of the Pilotage Commission. It will therefore be seen that section 442 is no longer operative. For the same reason all the powers with respect to pilotage in the Quebec district are now vested in the minister. The only portion of section 443, as it stands at present, that it is necessary to retain is that portion defining the number of pilots for the district; and that provides that the number shall not exceed 125.	.
That is the present law?

speechtext: That is exactly as the law stands at present.

On motion of Hon. W. J. Roche (Minister of the Interior), Bill No. 84, to authorize certain school and Dominion lands to be included in the Taber Irrigation district in the province of Alberta, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.
On section 1-short title:

Where is
this irrigation district?

It is in the constituency
represented by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Buchanan). It is not very far from the town of Lethbridge.

Is it on the
boundary line?
Not on the boundary'line,
About thirty miles from it.

The reason for the introduction of this Bill is that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have an irrigation district adjacent to the Taber district, and the people of the Taber district are desirous of availing themselves of the water privileges by the extension of the Canadian Pacific irrigation works into their district. Under the Alberta Act they have formed themselves into an irrigation district, that Act permitting them to bond their lands for the purpose of raising money for the extension of irrigation works. There are, within the Taber district, certain school lands which, of course, are administered by the Dominion Government in trust for the province. Some time ago the provincial secretary of the Government of Ablerta waited upon me and asked that this Bill be introduced, and the provincial Government sent forward an Order in Council making a request for this legislation. This Bill is to allow the school lands to be bonded in a similar manner to the patented lands, with this distinction that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have agreed to accept the bonds which are a first lien upon the patented lands, but that we are retaining our lien as a first lien on the school lands. That is the only difference between the patented lands belonging to private individuals and the school lands.

Section agreed to.

28C7
On section 2-school lands may be dealt with as other lands in irrigation districts :

As section 2 is worded, would it not prevent the district organizing, and bonding the lands for irrigation purposes on account of the permission that has to be secured from the owners of the land? Amongst the lands that are coming under the irrigation district there are certain school lands, which have been sold, but which are still really in the possession of the Dominion Government, and, according to this section, the consent of the owners or purchasers of the lands must first be obtained. There was a vote taken of tho-se within the boundaries of this particular district, and they availed themselves of the opportunity afforded under the Alberta Irrigation Act; but, as I read this section, it may delay the establishment of
4 p.m. this system if further consent has to be secured from these parties. I was wondering if the section could be drafted in sudlf a way as to enable them to proceed without that. A number of these parties live at distant points, so that it might take some time to secure their consent to the arrangement. I may, however, be wrong in my interpretation of the section.

It is necessary to obtain the consent of the purchasers of the school lands just as it is necessary to obtain the consent of the owners of patented lands. I do not think it would be proper to pass legislation until the consent of the owners of the school lands had been obtained. They, of course, have made certain payments on the school lands; but, as they have not completed their payments, we retain our lien as a first lien. I do not think that any appreciable delay will be occasioned by waiting to obtain their consent.
The vote taken last year did not include the holders of school lands.
I do not know whether the vote included the owners of school lands or not.
As I understand it, they are not really'the owners until they have completed the payments. Are there any school lands in the district that have not yet been disposed of?

There are 36,910 acres of land, of which 12,110 acres of school
lands have been sold, but not patented, and 1,100 acres are unsold and vacant.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported.

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT ROGERS (Minister of Public Wbrks):
speechtext: Before proceeding with the consideration of the Estimates in detail, I would like to say a word with respect to the Estimates of the Public Works Department generally. First, let me draw the attention of the committee to the fact that two years ago the Estimates of the department were the largest that had ever been presented by that department in the history of Canada, the amount being something like $48,000,000. A few months afterwards the war broke out, and it became necessary to reduce and economize as much as possible, and by the end of the year it w,as found that we had only spent about $29,000,000. At the session last year the Estimates were reduced from $48,000,000 to something like $34,000,000, a reduction of over $13,000,000. I am glad to be able to point out to the committee that we have expended only about $19,000,000, or about $15,000,000 less than was voted by Parliament last year, and about $10,000,000 less than last year's expenditure. The Estimates presented to-day amount to about $27,000,000, or $7,000,000 less than the Estimates presented last year; and it is hoped that at least $10,000,000, or perhaps a little more, will be left unexpended at the end of the year. That will mean that the Public Works Department will not expend more than $16,000,000 or $17,000,000 during the fiscal year 1916-17. I am speaking now, of course, of the main Estimates. I think these figures give evidence of the fact that the department has exercised and is exercising the greatest possible care, in view of present conditions, in dealing with the money voted by the House at the several sessions since the one before the outbreak of the war. I do not know that there is much to add. When we take up the items in detail, we shall be glad, as usual, to supply any information that we can give that will assist hon. members in their consideration of these votes.

I think the Minister of Public Works is to be congratulated on his effort to satisfy 
the House and the country that the Minister of Finance was in some sense right when he said, in effect, . that the Estimates foT this year were padded, and that there would be about $29,000,000 which it would not be necessary to expend. I and other members on this side of the House have made inquiry of the different ministers one after the other, tout not one of them has been able to give us any hope that there would toe a saving in his department. We are, therefore, very far away from the $29,000,000 that the Minister of Finance led us to toelieve would not toe expended, yet it is some consolation to receive the assurance of the Minister of Public Works that in his Estimates there are items aggregating about $10,000,000 which it will not be necessary to expend. Where the other $19,000,000 is to be found we hope the Minister of Finance will indicate before the session is finished.
I do not wonder that the Minister of Public Works has found it necessary to curtail expenditures for which he has made estimates. The Estimates are very, very large indeed. But they have been very large during the years my hon. friend has administered the department. I look at the report of the Minister of Public Works, and I find that in 1910-11, the last full year of the late Government, when I had the honour of being Minister of Public Works, the total expenditure, both on capital and on income account, was $11,807,035.42. There were many gentlemen on the floor of this House, many prominent gentlemen throughout the country, who thought that the Department of Public Works was, to use a common expression, "going some"at that time. I remember being very strongly criticised. I recall one very economical newspaper, the Toronto News, which spoke with amazement and horrOT of the "enormous expenditure" of the Department of Public Works, as evidence of unjustifiable and unheard of extravagance on the part of the minister of that day, and indicated that these expenditures could only' toe accounted for by the fact that the minister was reckless in the use of the public funds. But just see how expenditure increased when hon. gentlemen opposite got at the helm. In the following year, 1911-12, the total reached $13,928,026.87, and in 1913-14, it was $18,844,223.90, nearly double the expenditure of the last full year when I occupied the position of 'Minister of Public Works. In 1913-14, the actual expenditure jumped

to $27,991,336.94, or about two and a half times what it was in the last year I was minister.
They had got into their stride by that time.

Yes, they had got their gait. In 1914-15 the expenditure reached the enormous sum of $29,283,316.82, or pretty close to three times what it was in the year 1910-11. In 1910-11 it was $11,807,000, in round numbers; in 1914-15 it was $29,283,000. Yet for the greater part of the year 1914-15 the war was on. Gentlemen who occupy the treasury benches would have the country believe that they had been practically certain that there was danger of *a European conflict, danger of a great world war breaking out in which Canada would be called upon to participate. If these gentlemen honestly believed that, surely they must have anticipated that the financial resources of this country would be strained to the uttermost. Surely they must have anticipated that the war would be a most strenuous one, that vast expenditure would be involved and that vast obligations would necessarily be incurred. I think it will be difficult for hon. gentlemen occupying the treasury benches to satisfy their own consciences, still less the judgment of the people of this country, that they have not been exceedingly reckless in the expenditure of public mbneys. As I look over the public works which have been carried on throughout this country during the past three or four years I am not able to realize that there has been necessity for a very much greater annual expenditure than there w.as during the years that I was Minister of Public Works. The matter of expenditure on the part of the Government has been fully discussed on the Address and on the Budget, and therefore at this late stage in the session perhaps I should be uselessly faking up *time if I were to deal with the matter further. It is a deplorable fact that many hon. gentlemen sitting on the other side of the House whom I have had the pleasure of seeing here for a number of sessions of Parliament and who, when I was Minister of Public Works, were clamouring for economy, criticising expenditure, [DOT] making their eloquent voices heard in this House in stentorian tones, to^iay are silent- .silent as though they were struck dumb. Not one word of protest comes from them; it is left entirely to us upon this side of
the House to point out the extravagances and unwarranted expenditures which have been made by the ministers of the Crown.

There is not time for
anybody else to say a word.
I will give my hon. friend time now, if he wants it.
It is not time he wants; it is expenditures.

The Minister of Public Works having informed us that he will be able to get along with the moderate expenditure of about $17,000,000 during the current year, I think it would be well if he would consent to strike out of his Estimates of $27,000,000 the items which go to make up the $10,000,000 difference. I think it is a great mistake to keep in the Estimates amount's which it is not intended to . expend; it is not fair to Parliament and it is not fair to the country. Of course, I realize that the minister is human. I know that quite a number of gentlemen around him are interested in these imaginary public works which exist only on paper, in the sense that they are in the Estimates. Hundreds of items are revotes, showing that there is no urgency for the works in question. I know that the minister has a tender feeling for his supporters. He knows that it pleases them to take up the blue-book and see among the Estimates items which affect their own constituencies. He realizes that it would give them pleasure and advantage to go to their constituents, and, referring to these blue-books, point out to them that they succeeded after great effort in getting the minister to put these items in the Estimates, and that if they will only be patient', the time will come in the future-whether in the near future or in the distant future-when their expectations in regard to some of the public works mentioned in the bluebook will be realized. I would ask the minister if that is a proper course to take? Would it not be the proper course to at once strike out these items and simply ask the committee to vote for public works which are required in the public service and which it' is intended to proceed with during the current year? I would suggest that the minister strike out of these Estimates the sum of $10,000,000, which he does not want, the putting in of the items in connection with which is merely a waste of printers' ink, and the consideration of which, if we have to take them up item by item, will involve a good many hours, and, perhaps, days of the time

of this Parliament. I think a great deal would be gained by the minister's striking out the amount of $10,000,000.

My hon. friend did not understand me. What I said was that in respect to any public works where engage-*ments or commitments have been made, I am quite willing to have the amount remain; but if it is not intended to proceed with the public building to which the hon. gentleman refers, and which I recognize to be quite necessary, as Peterborough is a rapidly growing and important town, the mere placing of the amount in the Estimates does not help-
No.

-because the vote will expire on the 31st March next, and will have to be placed in the Estimates again. Therefore, striking it out now would make

no^difference. A record of it would be kept in the Department of Public Works, and when the time arrived when the minister thought the particular public work under consideration should be gone on with, he could give his instructions to the deputy minister, and the deputy could place the amount in the Estimates for the consideration of Parliament. Therefore nothing would be lost in -respect of the construction of the building, but the Estimates would be honest Estimates, showing what, in the expectation of the minister, will be required during the coming year.
Has it not always been the custom of every Government in Canada to insert such items in the Estimates?

I think not.
Some hon. MEMBERS : Oh, oh!
I think I can convince my hon. friend.

No, you cannot; I can
convince my hon. friend to the opposite.

My hon. friend cannot. I do not think a minister has ever before come down with Estimates and declared that it was not intended to spend any large sum of money such as the amount the minister refers to. It has occurred, that amounts have been placed in the Estimates for public works which it was intended- to carry on, but by reason of the engineers or architects being very busy, or of some other condition, it was not possible to proceed with the works, and the amounts have had to be re-voted during the next year. That is entirely different from the present case where, in consequence of the war, the minister states very frankly that there are some $10,000,000 in these Estimates for work which has not been commenced, to which' the country is in no way committed, and with which it is not intended to proceed during the coming year. I have never known a case where a minister, having made up his mind that a work should not be proceeded with during the coming year, has, nevertheless, put the amount in the Estimates. There has always been -a bona fide expectation that the work would be gone on with, that the land would be bought, or that the contract .would be let and the work proceeded with. Of course, even that would be interfered with by the circumstances to which I have referred.

I have listened with great interest to my hon. friend's comments on the Estimates for the Public Works Department, of which he has such a complete knowledge. I cannot agree with his statement that all the Estimates brought down to the House in any session are usually spent. If he will go over the record during his own period as Minister of Public Works, he will find every justification for the contradiction of his statement that came from this side of the House. I would draw his attention to the fact that in 1907-8 there was a difference of about $4,000,000
If I remember rightly, that was the year when the financial depression came on after Parliament rose.

We will take that for granted, and eliminate that year from consideration. Let us take the next year 190809. The estimated expenditure, according to the items brought down by my hon. friend that year, was $19,922,000, and he spent only something over $14,000,000, a difference of $6,000,000.
He was economical.

In 1910-11 the Estimate brought down was $17,000,000, and, as stated by my hon. friend, he spent only $11,000,000, a difference of $6,000,000 again. In 1911-12, which was the last year of my hon. friend's administraton, his Estimate was $24,301,000, and he spent only $14,300,000, or a difference of $10,000,000. If that rule applied in the reign of my hon. friend, it should apply to-day as well. However, I quite agree with my hon. friend that, owing to the war, conditions _ are rather different to-day than they were at that particular time. But then we must not lose sight of the fact that before the war broke out, the year before last, when these Estimates came down, these various items were placed in the Estimates in good faith; and with equal good faith the statement was made to this Parliament by myself, as Minister of Public Works, that there were many items in the Estimates that would not he gone on with in view of existing conditions. I think my hon. friend, on examination of the Estimates, will bear me out when I say that good faith has been kept by my department in that respect; and in the same sense I say that, having in good faith placed these amounts in the Estimates, and in good faith having announced that in view of the outbreak of the war there were many public undertakings that would not be carried out until such time as normal conditions returned,
we should at least keep good faith in allowing these items to remain in the Estimates. I think the hon. gentleman will, on reflection, see the reasonableness of that position taken by the department, and that he will entirely agree with me that it would be an act of bad faith on the part of the Public Works Department to strike from the Estimates the items that were placed there under the circumstances I have described. In view of the conditions caused by the war, we gave a pledge that a certain sum included in the Estimates of last year would not be spent. We have kept faith, and we make the same pledge this. year. There are various items that are re-votes, and it is understood that, unless special notice is given when any item is under consideration, such re-votes will not be expended during the coming year, especially if they are for new work. I think this explanation will satisfy my hon. friend.

I realize that in dealing with items for works which are actually under contract, and which have been considered on more than one occasion by the committee and the House, it would not be necessary to take up very much time, unless some hon. member might wish information on some special item which he might have in mind. But, in regard to the amounts to which the minister refers, a good many of them are revotes, some of which i observe are not-exactly the same as the original voted. There might be a difference in some cases of $1,000 or $2,000. Probably in some cases that might be accounted for by the fact that the site may have been purchased. I would like to have an expression of the view of the committee upon the general idea of the propriety of reducing the Estimates. I do not want to put the committee, or hon. gentlemen opposite, to the trouble of coming in specially to vote item by item, but I would like to teat the sense of the committee in respect to one item. Take the item, " Ottawa Archives building extension;" that is a revote, and it is not intended to go on with it during the coming year. " Ottawa-departmental block-addition "-
That-is a work under way.

Of course you would
have to go on with that. " Ottawa-new departmental buildings and sites therefor."
That is to pay the balance of the purchase price of the sites.

Of course that would
have to go on. " Ottawa-Parliament buildings-addition." That will have to be struck out; that will never be done.
I propose to move to strike that out.

" Toronto-new federal
buildings;" there is nothing done there, or if anything has been done, it must be very small, and nothing effectual can be done during the coming year. I would propose to strike out from those amounts which cannot be used, and I would therefore move that the proposed vote be reduced by the sum of $360,000. These are amounts which it is absolutely clear will not be required and out of which not one dollar will be expended during this year.
I told my hon. friend a moment ago that I proposed to strike out the item " Ottawa-Parliament buildings- addition $100,000." Therefore his estimate of the amount is incorrect.

Then my motion will be that the item under consideration be reduced by the sum of $260,000.
Motion negatived.

I think it has always been customary, previous to the advent of my hon. friend as Minister of Public Works, for the minister, when he came down with his Estimates, to give a full explanation of the expenditures of the .past year, and also of the moneys that were proposed to be expended during the coming year. My hon. friend comes down now with a proposition to vote $27,000,000, and he acknowledges that he proposes to expend at least $17,000,000 of that amount, or about $5,000,000 or $6,000,000 more than was found necessary or advisable five years ago, and he has given us practically no explanation. The little explanation my hon. friend did give was all on the line of trying to make this House and the country believe that he was such a very economical minister that he was asking for so many million dollars less than had been expended and less than had been asked during the past two or three years. But he did not explain that during the past two o$ three years under his management the expenditure has been abnormal, double and treble what it was five years ago. All these big expenditures have taken place at a time when the revenues of the country were very much decreased, and, during the last year and a half, when

we were engaged in a tremendous war. Neither my hon. friend the minister, nor those sitting behind him, seem to realize the position the country will be in. They are going on practically with the same lavish expenditures as ever. Why was it necessary, during the year 1914-15 and 1913-14, to expend $28,000,000 and $29,000,000 respectively, when five years ago, at a time when the revenues were buoyant, when the country was prosperous, we got along very well with an expenditure of $11,000,000 or $12,000,000? Does my hon. friend not realize the position this country is going to be in during the course of another year or two if this war goes on? There is every prospect of it going on for another year, and probably a good deal longer, and should that be the case we are going to have a war debt of at least $1,000,000,000. If by any chance the Government buy up a number of railways-and it is reported they are going to buy a railway in Quebec -if they take over the Canadian Northern railway, as they may have to, and if they take over the Grand Trunk Pacific, we are going to have another item of debt that is going to run very close to $1,000,000,000. With our present debt we are going to add over $2,000,000,000, and we are going to have to raise $100,000,000 this year to pay the interest upon the debt over and above the ordinary expenditures of the country. Instead of the minister realizing the situation, instead of realizing what is almost a certainty, that in a couple of years we shall have to provide $100,000,000 to pay the interest on our national debt, he refuses ab-* solutely to curtail the extravagance that has been going on. 'If people will not realize the position we are drifting into, something serious will take place, something will have to be done.
My hon. friend refuses to cut out the items for public buildings. I tell him that the day is coming very soon when we shall not be in a position to put up public buildings, no matter how badly they may be needed. Four out of five of these public buildings are absolutely unnecessary. I say that, fully realizing my responsibility as a member. My hon. friend from Peterborough spoke a few minutes ago of a public building in that town. Peterborough is a good town, and in good times, l,ike any other prosperous town, would be entitled to a public building, and we
5 p.m. should be glad to vote an item for it. The fact remains, however, that just as good accommodation can

be got in Peterborough, and in any other city, village or town, by renting a building; and it can 'be done for half what it costs to erect a building. I know that by experience. In my own constituency in certain towns the public is given as good accommodation as can be found anywhere in the Dominion. The rents paid for these buildings are fair .and moderate and it does not cost one-half what it costs in places where buildings are *put up by the department, on which interest on the cost has to be paid as well as heating and caretaking expenses. The country is coming to that point where it cannot afford to indulge in the extravagances of past years. I am not blaming one more than another for that. But conditions are changed; and the Government does not realize it, or if they do they do not .act as if they did. Now is the time to begin to curtail expenditures. But the Minister of Public Works asks us to vote $10,000,000 which he never intends to expend. I can quite understand that in such a large department it is impossible tofigureout to a dollar just what will be expended, but to deliberately ask Parliament to vote $10,000,000 which there is no intention of expending is something that has never been done before in this Dominion. It is a bad prece-' dent to establish, and a foolish thing to do. It is simply done for the purpose of making people in certain places believe they are going to get public buildings. I venture to say there are votes in these Estimates for public buildings that will not be put up during the next fifteen years, simply because we shall not be able to raise or borrow the necessary money. After a while the people of Canada will come to see that the Government are paying out millions of dollars for public buildings, when they could get just as good accommodation for half the cost by renting offices. If my hon. friend will persist in putting up public buildings, let me draw his attention to what they are doing in the United States. For many years past, and until recently, the United States have been following the system in vogue in this country, of putting up public buildings in a haphazard way, giving one town a certain class of building, and a much smaller town with a much smaller revenue, a much better building.
Not under this Government.

There was no system in it; it was simply a matter of political pull. But in the United States, within the past three years, or at all events quite recently, a great change has been brought about by the man in charge of their Public Works Department. He has adopted a system of standardized public buildings. A town of 50,000 inhabitants gets a building up to a certain standard, and costing a certain amount; towns between 50,000 and 100,000 get a building of a higher standard, and towns between 100,000 and 250,000 a higher standard still, and so on. The result has been, according to an article I read not very * long ago, and which went very fully into the matter, that the cost of public buildings in the United States has been reduced by just one-half, and the people are getting buildings much better suited to their requirements. So if the Minister of Public Works intends to go on putting up public buildings, I would suggest that he should inaugurate a similar system in Canada, and see if we cannot accomplish, here what has, been accomplished in the United States. I would much prefer, however, that he follow the suggestion of my hon. friend from St. John, of cutting out the items he does not intend to expend. There is no use mincing matters. These items are in the Estimates for one purpose, and one purpose only, and that is for a political purpose. They look well, and they may influence a few votes. In the past I believe that sort of thing has influenced a few votes, but I very much mistake the temper of the people of Canada if that sort of thing will influence votes in the future. I am not so sure that my hon. friend, who claims to know something about elections,-and we give him credit for that-would not make more votes if he cut out the items altogether that he does not intend to expend this year. I am sure that would meet with the approval of a great many people throughout this country. As I have said, we are not in a position to go on with these public buildings, and we shall not be in a position to go on witli them for many years to come. What money we shall be able to raise and borrow wi be needed for a very different purpose

for the purpose of paying the interest ( our debt, and undertaking public work that are really needed. Many of the public buildings provided for in the Estimates this year are really not needed, and only in good times when money was plentiful should

we be justified in putting them up. Under present conditions, it would be absolutely criminal to think of putting up these buildings, and therefore it is foolish to think of keeping the items in the Estimates.

I fancy my hon. friend
was not in the House when the committee started its work, or he would have heard the statement I made, and which covered most of the points he has raised.
I would like to say, in respect to a new point raised by my hon. friend that as, since the outbreak of the war, some of our architects have not been busy, we have devoted a considerable amount of attention to the question of standard buildings, and we have prepared standard plans for public buildings for towns of various sizes. When we proceed to erect new buildings in different parts of the Dominion, those plans will be used as the standard. I am sorry that my hon. friend has gone the length of making the extravagant statements he has made about the condition of the country, and which are not borne out by the facts.
The statements are more true than extravagant.

It would be hard to find greater evidence of economy and of an appreciation of existing conditions than is exhibited by the Estimates which I have presented. My hon. friend has spoken about the conditions of five years ago when hon. gentlemen opposite were in power. The estimates presented m that year by the Public Works Department amounted to $14,500,000; this year I have assured the House that the expenditure on public works will not be more than $16,000,000 or $17,000,000. That is a very creditable showing in view of the changed conditions in Canada. Confidence having been restored by the return of the present Government to power, there was naturally a great development and a consequent great necessity for public undertakings. The minister is absolutely
mistaken, because rent is paid for the building, which 'is owned by the Mount Allison institution.

I think I can help the
minister a little. With respect to buildings in the smaller villages or towns, the postmaster himself pays the rent and gets an allowance from the Post Office Department. Sometimes, in the case of larger towns, the Public Works Department pays rental, but ordinarily the Postmaster General makes an allowance for the rental of the smaller buildings.
It may be done that way, but it is a fact that rent for this building is paid to the Mount Allison institution. T.he department did not buy the building, because the building is to be taken away.

$8,000, I think.
Mr.- ROGERS: We are not paying any rent so far as we know in our department.
It may be done in a roundabout way, as the hon. member for St. John suggested, but it is a fact that rent and interest are being paid.

The amount which is allowed to postmasters in smaller places for rental is often inadequate. I know that I used to urge on the former Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) that if the Postmaster General would, increase the allowance to the postmaster the Public Works Department could save a vast amount of money, and would be saved from acceding to demands for new public buildings. However, I never could get my hon friend, with his

economic views, to accede to my wishes. It may be that the present Postmaster General is the same.

Part of this building is used as a custom house, and rent is paid for it by the Customs Department. If the postmaster pays the rent for the building the amount is included in his salary; it is simply paid over in that way.

The fact remains that the Government, through the Post Office Department or the Customs Department, are paying the same rent now for the building that they paid before they purchased the lot. Five per cent on the purchase price of the lot, $8,000, would be $400 a year, and to this extent the Government are paying more for the building than they were paying prior to the purchase of the lot. I do not think the minister ought to ask us to pass this item until he can find out whether that is so, and, if it is, he should give assurance to the committee that it will be remedied. It is absurd that after paying $8,000 on account of the land, we should go on paying the same rent for the building that we paid before.

The Department of Customs and the Post Office Department in many cases pay their own rents. It is true that we have bought a lot upon which there is a building, but we did not buy the building. The building belongs to the Mount Allison institution, and of course they have a perfect right to rent it.

And you have the right
to charge them rent for the land.

The land was bought a couple of years ago, before the outbreak of war, and no effort has been made since that time towards starting the public building. Sack-ville is a very good town; a public building there was necessary. It will be gone on with as soon as we possibly can, but not during the present year,

As to the allowance
made to the postmasters for rental, I think the minister will find that it is based not upon the actual value of the building, but upon the revenue of the office. The amount which is allowed to the postmaster is not often more than $40 or $50 a year.

The fact remains that
the Government still pay the same rents, after having paid $8,000 on the property.

Part of it was bought when I was minister and part by the late Hon. Mr. Monk. I thought it would not exceed about $400,000. The contractors are the Rhodes-Curry Company, Limited. Is any legislation contemplated which will relieve Senator Curry, who is president of the company, from the provisions of the Independence of Parliament Act? incorporated company, to engage upon any public work under contract with the Government. That applies to senators and to members of the House of 'Commons. It would be pretty bard bn Senator Curry if somebody chose to .proceed against him. He would be liable to a penalty of $200 a day for all the time he has been sitting in the Senate since this contract was entered into.

That is a very difficult

I may say, however, that we make it a rule not to put up a public building in any town unless it has a population of at least 1,000. Our plan is that for a town of that size a $5,000 building should be sufficient and for a town having a population of 2,000 a building costing probably $10,000-keeping the cost as low as we possibly can. Those are the instructions that I have given to the architects ih preparing plans for public build-[DOT] trigs for the future when we shall be ready to carry them on.

Will my hon. friend
make that rule applicable to all places having the population stated?

We treat all places alike. Of course, conditions vary to some extent. Some towns in Eastern Canada. may remain stationary for a very long time so far as population is concerned, whereas with towns in the Western country there may be a very good prospect of conditions in the future being such as to require increased accommodation. A public building costs a little more in the West than it does in the East. Having due regard, however, to the general conditions, we are endeavouring to follow the rule as closely as possible.

I would point out that even in the West the towns have a habit of growing either way; some grow more populous and some less populous. In my judgment no place having a population of less than 5,000 should have a public building. $5,000 or $10,000 is cheap for a Government public building, but the cost of repairs, caretaking and heating is considerable, and in a case where such a building is erected in a small town the cost is three or four times as great as the cost of accommodation which would be sufficient for all the needs of the community. In view of the tremendous fixed charges that we shall be called upon to bear, I think it would be well for both sides of the House to agree on a definite policy in this matter. We should have a fixed rule-because it occurred when our people were in power just as it has with the present Government -and avoid having public buildings costing from $10,000 to $25,000 in places where there are less than 1,000 inhabitants. To do this is to expend Government funds in an absolutely wasteful manner.

During the past two years we have adopted the principle of renting as much as possible. I am sure that that will continue for some time, to come, in order to avoid as far as possible the construction of public buildings.

We do not waste so much time in the House and the country saves on that.

The amount is more than ten times the amount spent in Nova Scotia although the population of Ontario is not more than five or six times the population of Nova Scotia. The same comparison exists as between Ontario and the other provinces. If there is any special reason why this enormous sum should be spent in Ontario, twice as much as is spent in Quebec and three or four time as much as in the other provinces in proportion to population, I think it would be well for the minister to state it. If it can be justified I suppose the minister can do it.

It is very easy indeed for me to give my hon. friend an answer to the question which he asks. The needs in Toronto have been neglected for some time. We are trying to correct that condition of affairs in regard to the requirements of the public service in Toronto and as we go along we will find that' the large items for necessary undertakings in Toronto and the customs building at Ottawa account for the difference that may appear in the sum total as against the other provinces. In Toronto Postal Station A will take $465,000,, and the Toronto customs building $500,000. That makes practically $1,000,000 for necessary work in Toronto. It is securing three

It does seem a waste of time for a lot of able-bodied men to be sitting here shouting "carried" to items that the minister tells us he is not going to expend. It must look curious to the public who are furnishing the money.
The war may be over in May, and then we may start with the buildings.
Pass the whole bunch at once, then.

That would be being foolish in a lump instead of by sections. I am not sure that the public we represent will think this a very businesslike proceeding. Suppose that some of us who pretend to know something about business were estimating our requirements for the coming year, and if we put down the same amount that we expended two years ago, and took the estimate to the bank and asked for credit, the bank would say: "This is too high for war time," and then if we said: "Oh, I am not going to spend all this, but I want credit for the whole amount," the bank would say, "Go back and revise your estimate; and put in just what you really intend to spend, like any business man would, and then we will give you a line of credit." But we are not doing that; we are voting millions that we are assured will not be expended, and to my mind that seems very unbusinesslike.

These items were put in
the Estimates in good faith, believing there was a necessity for the buildings in the different cities and towns mentioned. We now say, in all good faith: We are not going on with these public buildings while the war continues, but we will retain the votes in

the Estimates in the hope that we shall be able to go on with the work as soon as the war is over. Believing, as we do, that it is in the public interest that these buildings should be erected, it would be ill-advised on the part of this Parliament to drop the items from the Estimates, and it would be misunderstood by those who are not so well acquainted with the actual conditions as we in this Parliament are, or at all events, should be. We say to the people interested in the construction of these buildings in the different cities and towns: the work will not be undertaken during the continuance of the war, but as soon as possible thereafter.

In view of the financial commitments this country has bad to make on account of the war, and the taxation that has been imposed upon business for the first time, does the minister think that if the war finished in June or July next, we should be able to spend any money on these buildings?
Mr. ROGER'S: If the war were to end in June or July-and let us hope it will- there might be some hope of going on with the buildings more urgently needed; but then will be time enough for us to consider whether or not we should go on with them. Present conditions are serious in many respects, but not so serious that we shall not be able to cope with them. We have great confidence in the future of this country. This Parliament is expected, in the matter of public works necessary for the public service, to keep pace with private enterprise throughout the Dominion. That is the line we take, and those are the prospects we have, and that is why, in my humble judgment, the items should remain in the Estimates, where they can certainly do no harm. I think it would be an evidence of weakness to give up hope of going on with the construction of these buildings.

If the war should stop now, does the minister seriously think that our financial condition is such that we could afford to spend money on luxuries? Is the minister not aware that if the war did stop immediately, and if the immense expenditure for munitions and war supplies ceased it would be found necessary for Canada to economize very much more than she is doing at present? That is the exact situation, and my hon. friend must know that if these items are left in the Estimates the people in the districts
affected are going to be misled if they are told that amounts are voted for the construction of public buildings or public works which cannot be gone on with. The Government cannot find in all the history of the British Parliament any precedent for sums of money being placed in the Estimates and voted prima facie to be expended1 when the Chancellor of the Exchequer knew that it was absolutely impossible to spend them.

We are not proposing the construction of any work that is regarded as a luxury, as my hon. friend has stated, and, since the outbreak of the war, we have been economizing as closely, I am sure, as it would be possible for any department to do. At the same time I have a greater confidence and a greater hope in the future of Canada than apparently my hon. friend has. I am confident that, should the war come to an end during the summer months, then the condition of Canada and of the Canadian people will be much better than he anticipates. We 'are in as-strong a position as any country in any part of the civilized world, and we will be able to carry on our public works in the public interest in every case as the necessity arises. Therefore, I do not think there is any gloomy outlook for the Canadian people. We look with hope to the future and with the feeling that if the war should come to an end during the present year the money which has been spent in carrying on the war will be felt very lightly by reason of the great advantage which will accrue to Canada at the close of the war from the fact that we have such immense opportunities for the attraction of immigration, and for the building up of a greater and stronger country. While the war conditions of to-day might bear heavily upon seven or eight million people, with the prospects that we have of having a population of ten, twelve or fifteen million people within a few years, the cost and burden of the war will bear but lightly upon them, and I look forward to expansion rather than to that istagnation which my hon. friend fears. I look forward to a very different prospect at the close of the war, and we have all very good reason to hope for better conditions in the future than we have had in the past.

My hon. friend is
certainly an optimist, but I do not think some of his colleagues will take his remarks very seriously. The Minister of Trade and

Commerce (Sir George Foster) was by no means optimistic about the future of Canada; he did not take the view that his colleague the Minister of Public Works does. I would like to hear from my hon. friend, who has dilated with such beautiful optimism about the certainty of so many people coming to Canada during the next few years, where they are going to come from. My hon. friend must face these problems seriously and not indulge in mental gymnastics.

I hope my hon. friend
has taken note of what so eminent a man as Lord Derby has had to say with respect to the prospects after the war. He has told the English people that there will undoubtedly be a large immigration to the overseas dominions; that the people who have been working in offices in England and who [DOT]have gone to the war, will never be satisfied to remain in European countries; that they will come to the overseas dominions in the hope, if nothing else, of finding a more peaceful country in which to rear their families in comfort. No portion of the overseas dominions presents so many attractions to intending immigrants as does this Dominion. We have in the western provinces in the neighbourhood of 3,000,000 acres of land, the finest in the world, that have not yet been touched; we have in the Prairie Provinces land sufficient to take care of the whole population of Great Britain. Therefore I think we have good reason to look forward with hope to brighter and better conditions in this country at the close of the war.

I am very much pleased at the optimism of my hon. friend and I hope he is correct in his belief, but it is well to be on the safe side. My hon. friend hopes that this is to be a country where the conquest of peace will be the ideal, and that is one reason he gives why immigration will come to us from European countries. If we are to present that ideal in a practical form to intending immigrants, we shall have to be careful when the war is over to keep on our shoulders very level heads and to see that we are not stampeded and diverted from what ought to be our natural aspirations as a country with peace as our chief aim. Undoubtedly we shall be confronted with a school of thought that will regard it as necessary that Canada should be an armed nation as if war were imminent at any time. If that thought were allowed to

prevail, Canada would have no attractions to offer to- the intending immigrant over those of European countries. It will be a strong incentive for people in devastated European countries to come to our shores if they know that they are to be in a better position here as regards liability to war than they are in their own countries. So, one of the problems we shall have to deal with when this war is over is to counteract, so far as necessary, the inclination to make Canada a military country, with all that that means. We shall always have to have a certain preparedness, as becomes the dignity of a nation; tout it will be our duty also to guard against being stampeded into making Canada an armed camp,. That is one extreme; of course, there is the extreme on the other side. My hon. friend has given- me an opportunity to express this view, as I have expressed it elsewhere. I am not so optimistic about immigration- to- Canada immediately after the war as some people seem' to toe. It will take a little time for things to settle down, so-that Canada can present her proper attractions before the world. European countries that have been devastated will have to toe rebuilt, and the scarcity of men in those lands will leave all the fewer to come to Canada. It is all the more important, then, that we should have something much better to offer them than that which was offered in their o-wn land. Another idea I have is this. If we are to attract immigration, Canada must continue to assume her full Responsibility of self-government. I am afraid that we are becoming more of a child in some respects, wishing to lean on the Motherland for advice as well as for action, when we ought to depend upon ourselves. But that is a large question, and I will not go into it now.

I am glad to hear my hon. friend speak in the strain in which he has addressed the committee. It is true that we in Canada have always; been a peace-loving people. We are like the great Empire to which we belong, a great, contented, industrial, and peace-loving country. As that has been our position in the past, I am sure it will also be in the future. As for present conditions and the circumstances of to-day, I am sure there is no man in this House, and few in the Dominion of Canada, who dont realize that there was no place for the loyal citizens of Canada other than in this conflict. We have

taken part in this war in the full and confident belief that such was the will of a united Canadian people. But, while we have taken this course in order to meet conditions as they were, yet, at the close of this war, after we have succeeded, as I am sure we shall succeed, and as I am sure every hon, member of this House believes we shall succeed, in achieving a glorious victory for the cause for which we stand, we shall return to our own place, that of a peace-loving country not looking for war and not guided by war conditions, but desirous of building up a happy, prosperous, and progressive nation, and using as fully as we may the possibilities of our country, possibilities such as no other portion of the civilized world presents. The opportunities Canada will offer for peaceful labour will be such as must attract immigrants to our shores, and it will be our duty to lend every assistance within our power to make these immigrants prosperous and contented in the homes which they build here for themselves and their children .

I hope the hon. minister does not imagine that I was talking of present conditions when I spoke of peace, though that is what I would gather from his remark. I was discussing the future, when we shall be looking to Europe for the best class of immigrants. There are no two voices in Canada-or, if there be, the second .is so small that it is not heard-as to not only our duty, but our privilege to be in this war. My own view is that Canada's place would be in this war even if she were not a part of the British Empire at all. If we are to assume the dignity and responsibility of a nation; if we are to aspire to be leaders in establishing what we believe to be right for the welfare of the world, it is our duty to participate ih this war. I agree with everything the hon. minister has said as to the hopes and aspiration of Canada for the future, and I believe with him that victory must crown the efforts which the Allies are putting forth, and that the results of that victory will be a wider outlook for the nations of the world. The real result of this conflict will be no exclusive good for the British Empire or for the Allies," but general good for the entire world, in which Germany will participate as one of the greatest beneficiaries.
May I ask if this building at Dunnville is to be an immigrant building or a drill hall?

Oh, he should not do
that.

The hon. member for South Renfrew to-night portrayed conditions that might very seriously affect this country in the reconstruction period after the war. Is it not well to have these public works provided for, so that tlie labouring men, the builders, the mechanics of this country, and every person whose work tends to upbuild the industrial and national life, will, by the aid

of the Government, have something in dull times to keep the wolf from the door? I suppose the only reply is that the minister has said that he is not going to use this money, and Ontario is not to get anything out of it.
The hon. member for North Perth is a joker. He wanted to indulge in a little byplay for the amusement of the committee.

The member for
North Perth did not do the Minister of Public Works the honour of listening to What he was saying with regard to this matter. The idea is absurd
because if the war did	come to
an end, it would not be possible, in the financial condition of the country, to spend this money in any province, Nova Scotia as well as Ontario. Anything that I said I desire to repeat in regard to the items affecting my province, as well-as in regard to those affecting Ontario. ' To the suggestion that there was no sense in putting these items in the Estimates when the amounts are not to be spent, the member for North Perth says that it is a splendid thing to have them there; that it is pleasant for the labourers and contractors to think that some day they are going to have a chance to spend this money. On a former occasion this session I called attention to the splendid record which had been made by students of that college, a record which reflected credit on every province of Canada. I do not want to press unduly what I consider would be a proper thing, namely, the immediate construction of this building; but I think its construction would be justified because of the pressing necessity for the enlargement of the buildings for drilling purposes. I hope that the Minister of Public Works and all members of this House will visit that institution during the coming summer, and that in the very near future the Government will be in a position to thoroughly renovate the old Royal Military College building, in which the class rooms are situated, as the rooms are not now large enough for the number of students in attendance.
What is the attendance?

It varies, especially
since the outbreak of the war as it is almost impossible to keep the students there. There should be more accommodation. A splendid course is given and given at a reasonable cost. The college has been well called the West Point of Canada, and I trust that every member will be able to visit it and judge for himself what should be done to make the buildings all that they should be.

The statements made by my hon. friend are not new to me. I have heard them not only from himself but also from the Militia Department who have urged the necessity for this particular work. That is why, when the item was reached, I at once informed the committee that there was a very pressing necessity for the carrying out of this work, and I hear the same thing from young men from all parts of Canada who go there to take training. There is a general complaint of lack of accommodation.

If it will be any encouragement to the minister, I may say that I endorse everything that has been said by the hon. member for Frontenac, although he and I are not noted for agreeing. This building does not come within the category of ordinary public buildings which should not be proceeded with during war time. This is a war time building. If the Royal Military College is to continue to be the success it has been-and it is only within the last three or four years that we have learned how great that success has been-it Will be necessary to spend not only this small sum but perhaps more to keep it up to the standard that the Militia Department think it ought to be kept up. I should not consider that building at all in the category of ordinary public buildings, and I think that no objection could be taken to the minister departing from his rule in this case.

Ottawa-new drill hall, $50,000.

This is one of the old hardy annuals. I do not know when we started in with this new drill hall but I see that it appears in the Estimates for 1912-13, 1913-14, 1914-15, 1915-16, and 1916-17. This is the fifth time that we have been asked to vote this item for the same amount of $50,000 and it was voted three times before the war. The minister has explained the reason why these buildings are not being proceeded with, why so many are put in the Estimates so often, by saying that the war has prevented the construction of them, and it will be interesting to know why we are asked to vote this among others from year to year with no progress being made towards the construction of it.

There is a good deal in what my 'hon. friend says but the explanation is that when the item was originally placed in the Estimates there was a difficulty in connection with the selection of the site. The Department of Public Works only undertakes the construction of such buildings as these when the site has been selected by the Department of Militia and Defence. It has not been settled yet. We are simply 'carrying out the recommendation that has been made to us but nothing has been done and nothing will be done this year.	[DOT]

I regret to hear the minister say that nothing will be done because, while I fully appreciate the fact 'that the strictest economy should be practised during war time, I was glad to approve of the minister when he said that improvements would be made at Kingston. I would place in a similar class the drill hall at Ottawa. Ottawa is the capital of Canada and perhaps more soldiers congregate here for temporary drilling than elsewhere. Every hon. gentleman in the House knows perfectly well that the present drill hall is not adequate. It is a disgrace to the city. This is a case in which the minister should see that the site question is settled at once and that a new building is given to Ottawa.

We have the old drill hall, which is not very satisfactory. The site is entirely a matter for the Department of Militia and Defence arid we have not yet been informed that they have selected a site. I have no doubt the delay has been due primarily to that difficulty. Then, in addition, a great deal of expenditure has been necessary and has taken place in connection with militia in Ottawa and we have endeavoured to economize as much as we could and to get along, if possible, with the old drill hall. Could the Minister of
Public Works give us any. information as to the progress that is being made toward the reconstruction of the Parliament buildings? I understood, although I have no inside information, that a suggestion has been made for the formation of a committee of members of the House, possibly of the Upper Chamber as well, to assist, and advise in connection with the reconstruction. Has that committee been appointed, have any steps been taken to let the contract, is a contract to be let, is it to be done by force account, have the plans been finally approved-any information of that kind would be interesting.

I proposed a couple of
weeks ago that a committee consisting of three members from each side of the House should be named.
I asked the Prime Minister to name three, and the right hon. leader of the Opposition three. The Prime Minister has chosen Hon. Dr. Reid, Hon. Mr. Blondin, and Hon. Senator Lougheed, and I expect to get three names from the leader of the Opposition to-morrow morning. As soon as I receive these we will proceed to the consideration and final acceptance of the plans. We had an exhibition of the plans here and I am glad to be able to say that I have not yet heard a single complaint from any hon. gentleman as to the general layout as shown on the sketch. The work of this Committee 178	'
will be to give thorough consideration to all details, and to take into consideration, in conjunction with the members of the House, the division of the space. In the meantime, the architects are working out the details of the plan, and getting 10 p.m. everything ready as rapidly as possible. I hope that in a few days we shall be able to proceed with whatever plans the committed thinks best. Like my hon. friend, I think the building should be built on some kind of force account.

Will the.committee have control of the business end of the work, with power to let contracts/ appoint inspectors, and generally supervise the erection of the building? Or will they simply be an advisory committee to consult with the minister in regard to the plans? I should like to know just what powers they will have.
When I made the proposal for the appointment of the committee, I made a very full statement as to their powers. It is on Hansard, and I will send it over to my hon. friend.

I see they are building
a wooden tower on the old building.
That had to be done anyway, in order to clean things up.
Might I suggest that a great deal of room was taken up in the old building with what-I will not call it the bar-
Say restaurant.

I should not call it a
drinking room.	*
I object to that expression.
As we passed a prohibition measure the other day, I hope Parliament will set an example to the country by doing away with any room of that kind; we could use the space for rooms.

In the new building there will be a restaurant where meals will be served for the convenience of hon. members. That is my view, at all events, and I shall be glad to suggest it to the committee. Beyond that, I have no recommendations to make. If my hon. friend has anything to suggest, we shall be glad to hear him at the committee.
There has been no bar there for very many years.
Quite so. I am surprised that my hon. friend from Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) should have got the idea that such a thing existed in the old building.

I was talking to a leading contractor the other day, and he suggested that there were two portions of the new building that might be let by contract.
I am not aware to which portions he referred. Owing to conditions existing between parts of the old building, and on account of more tearing down to be done, perhaps it would be impracticable to let the contract for these two portions. This man is a successful contractor; I discussed it with him for quite a while, and told him that I would mention his suggestion to the minister.

Many suggestions and recommendations have been made to me, and it was primarily for the reason of dealing with these that I suggested the appointment of a committee. When the committee meets all these various suggestions and recommendations that I have received from many sources will be laid before them and considered.

There is one point in connection with the building that I hope the minister will not forget, and that is the acoustics. It is a curious thing, but architects in this country do not seem to understand that question. Most of the buildings that have been erected in my experience have been defective in that respect; this building we are sitting in now, for example. When we first came here, before the curtains were put up, we could hardly hear at all, even although the building was designed by* the best architects, probably, as it was intended for a national museum.
The animals were not supposed to talk.

If that was the best the architects could do, I think the minister should look somewhere else for a man who understands this important question. Acoustics and ventilation are two of the most important things to be considered in a chamber. I know that it is a difficult question, and that mistakes have been made in some of the greatest buildings in the world. In Sir Henry Lucy's description of the Houses of Westminster, he tells how both the Commons and House of Lords Chambers were very defective in their acoustic properties. The House of Commons had to be almost made over again before the members could hear one another.
The House of Lords was left as it was, and Sir Henry Lucy, who has spent most of his life in these Chambers, says that, with very few exceptions, the voices of the members of the House of Lords do not carry across the Chamber, that there have been perhaps only half a dozen members whose voices would carry across the Chamber. If great buildings in Europe are defective in this respect, great care will have to be taken if we are to have perfect acoustics in the new building on the Hill. I regard this as very important, and I know the minister does himself. Many of the men who come here are middle-aged, and some of them a little older, and it is therefore necessary that the acoustics should be good.
I would suggest that the acoustics be made like those of the House of Lords.
Judging from the remarks of my hon. friend from Guysborough, he takes a very keen and lasting interest in the Upper Chamber.
That seems to be a disease.

I agree with my hon. friend that in a general way the acoustic properties of a building are really the most important part of the whole work. I am glad to be able to tell him that the architects who have been selected are gentlemen who have travelled throughout the United States, England, France and other countries, and have already made thorough inspections of the public buildings in those countries, giving special consideration to the question of acoustics, and I understand they are satisfied that they will be able to make the chambers for the House of Commons and the Senate satisfactory in that respect. I am sure, from what I know of the two gentlemen so selected, that they are worthy of out confidence as to carrying out the work in the best manner possible and to the satisfaction of the House of Commons and of the Senate.

I hope the minister will impress upon the architects not to forget the ventilation, which I think is even more important than the acoustic properties. The latteT may 'be more important in some instances, but the ventilation is most important for our health. As I do not expect to be around very long, I hope the ventilation will be good.

I am sorry that my hon. friend should feel at this early stage in

the history of the country that it was time for him to pronounce his valedictory. Of course I can appreciate the fact that we had very poor ventilation in the old chambers, because they were on the inside. According to the present plan of the new building, the House of Commons and Senate chambers will be on the outside with windows, and every precaution possible will be taken for the proper ventilation of the building.

station.

We have been threatened with that new railway station so long that the people are curious about it. I believe that steps have been taken to start the new building. Or, perhaps I should say that symptoms of starting are shown.

This is a revote of $455,000 required for the erection of a new terminal postal station, as part of the easterly wing of the new union station, which is being built in accord with an Order in Council dated September 1, 1915. The hon. member understands that part of it probably better than I do. This is a part of the work on the terminal station in Toronto, and the work is going on. But there is no work
going on.
