I don't know where.
It is just starting.

The hon. minister will
not need to go very fast to keep pace with the work on the Toronto union station. The contract has been let, or a portion of it, and the public are hoping that the work will go on in a practical way from now forward. The present Toronto station is about the poorest excuse for a modern station that is to be found in any big city on the continent of America. A stranger needs a guide there, or he is liable to be run over by a train. If I were to put in a bill on a per capita basis for the people I have guided to safety out of that station, I am afraid I should be looked upon as a grafter.

If the railway companies proceed with no greater rapidity this year than in the past few months, the Government will not need to expend much money, for, of course, they will only spend it as the construction of the railway terminals proceeds, for they cannot do away with the old facilities until opportunity is afforded to provide the new. The minister said to-night that Toronto had never received much aid for any new buildings. I have been in public life for a good many years, and never objected to an item for Toronto, in fact, I have favoured it.
I do not think it would be fair-putting it on the lowest ground, I do not think it would be good polities-for any party to refuse to recognize a city of the importance of Toronto. While there has been no vote for this building until recently, the reason was that the Board of Railway Commissioners had ordered a new station to be built, but, unfortunately, it was some time after the order was passed before there was any semblance of it being enforced. Owing to conditions between the railway companies they only arrived at the point of starting recently. But there is this to be said, at present it is difficult for railway companies to secure money for improvements which are not direct revenue-producers, and a new railway station, while it provides extra accommodation for the public, does not produce directly any more revenue than the old station. I hope the railway companies will act as rapidly as they can in the construction of the union station and other terminal facilities that are being provided. These improvements are certainly needed in the city of Toronto. We in the province of Ontario, no matter how badly Toronto may treat,, us at election times, are proud of the city and of the progress it is making. The minister will not find any objection on this side to treating Toronto fairly and giving her what she requires in the public interest.

I entirely agree with what the hon. member for South Renfrew has said. A work of thie kind is usually delayed by reason of the fact that there are so many conflicting interests. The railway people have knowledge of the fact that the Government are ready to do their part so far as the portion of the (building to be used by the Government is concerned. It was about a year ago, perhaps less, that they gave evidence of being ready to start with the work, and we at once made it clear that we were ready to carry ox. our

part of the work. I understand that the foundation is now being proceeded with and that work is going ahead in earnest. We hope that it will be completed as rapidly as possible. I entirely concur with what my hon. friend has said, that the station in the city of Toronto is undoubtedly a disgrace to the railways that have to use it. It is in the public interest that we have this postal station there, and I am glad to know that our providing the necessary sum for carrying out that work meets with my hon. friend's approval.

I was pleased to hear
the member for Frontenac say that he had asked for a public building in proportion to the size of the place in which it was proposed to be erected, and, I assume, in proportion to the revenue. My idea is that these buildings should be erected only in proportion to the amount of the revenue. As the minister himself said a little while ago, a great many of these towns have
arrived at their full extent'. I could name dozens of them in Ontario that have not improved during the last 25 years; as a matter of fact, some of them have gone back. Some of the buildings in connection with which items were passed to-night- although they are not to be built this year, it is proposed that they shall be built sometime-and which cost from $25,000 to $30,000 are to be erected in villages having a population of about a thousand people. In such places the revenue could not be more than $1,200 or $1,300, and the present expenses not more than $300 or $350, including the postmaster's salary. I have gone through the post office reports very frequently, and I find that the expenses of these smaller offices generally run from $350 to $600 or $700. If we put up a building costing $25,000 it costs almost as much to light it and to heat it during the winter as it did to maintain the old office, postmaster and all. If the Government, no matter which party be in power, would establish the principle of erecting only a certain kind of building in small towns and villages, I do not think any fault could be found with erecting in a small village, the very best house in which would hardly cost more than from $2,500 to $4,000, a public building costing $3,000 to $5,000. It is quite probable that in such case the service given before-probably in a store or part of a store-was just as good as it would be in the new building. Expenditure of this kind is abnormal and in my judgment absolutely unnecessary.
The member for Frontenac has set a very good example; we have tried to follow it as closely as we can.

I hope the minister is in earnest.
